_about: Flame Atlas prepared answers (Team Flame Atlas, NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026). Answers to the questions the dashboard's buttons ask, written in advance with an AI assistant (Claude) from the team's curated NASA documents and tests table, and checked against the cited source pages in a second AI pass; same format as the live chat's answers. Every point names its source and page.

answers.question: Why did test BRE:20247A1 (Ethylene-nitrogen gas (burner), 40% O2) burn?

data.text: Ethylene-nitrogen on the 50 mm burner, ISS microgravity, quiescent air, 40% O2, 107 kPa: it burned the whole test until fuel shut-off, with oscillations beginning earlier (FTO); Table F.1 gives oscillation time 24.90 s and extinction time 150.93 s.

For the 50 mm ethylene-nitrogen tests of Table F.1, the author's model estimated flame temperatures (radiative-fraction correlation, Eq. 6.17) to judge whether the flames could reach steady state; all fell below the 1100–1200 K critical range.

inferred.text: In Table F.1 oxygen alone does not separate the outcomes: the tests that burned to fuel shut-off ran at 33–40% O2 and those that self-extinguished at 24–35% O2, all at 104–108 kPa in quiescent air.

other_side.note: no test on this burner self-extinguished above 35% O2

lead.text: BRE:20247A1 (50 mm burner, ISS microgravity, quiescent air, 40% O2, 107 kPa) burned until fuel shut-off, with oscillations beginning earlier; the thesis gives no test-by-test cause.

answer.not_covered: This test's fuel heat of combustion and mass flux are not in the tests table.

data.text: The 0g maximum oxygen concentration (MOC) of Ultem 1000 10 mil film in a microgravity drop-tower rig, 70.3 kPa, 30 cm/s concurrent flow: 23% O2, the highest oxygen at which a flame went out in the drop.
Each 5 × 10 cm sample was lit by a hot wire in 1 g in enriched oxygen; the test gas reached it shortly after the 5.18 s drop began, leaving the flame about 5 s in it.

The report's Fig. 4 shows concurrent flames at about 30 cm/s surviving the drop at about 23 and 22% O2, beside others that went out (read from the figure); its caption says near the boundary the same conditions can yield different results.

This is the report's own drop-tower result; a 2012 paper reprints the 23% O2 value as earlier data. The authors call these limits a conservative measure of the 0g limits, since some flames might go out given longer.
